newsitem.title: USA: Emergency Mideast summit opens at White House.
newsitem.headline: Emergency Mideast summit opens at White House.

text.p: President Bill Clinton welcomed Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to the White House under heavy security and secrecy rules on Tuesday to start a Middle East crisis summit with Israeli and Arab leaders.

Preceding Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat into a set of private meetings with Clinton, Netanyahu arrived at the White House cocooned in a caravan of police security vehicles and proceeded directly to the Oval Office unseen by reporters as part of an announced plan to minimise public statements.
Arafat, who had Clinton's ear right after the Israeli on the two-day summit agenda, conferred first at a Washington hotel with third summit guest King Hussein of Jordan.

He was seen driving to a hotel basement entrance preceded and followed by black security vans with automatic weapons poking out of the windows -- a highly unusual public display of security firepower in Washington.

Clinton called the summit in a desperate bid to prevent the Middle East peace process from collapsing amid the sudden resumption last week of bloody Israeli-Palestinian violence in the West Bank and Gaza.

But the heavy backdrop of U.S. election-year politics was immediately apparent as Netanyahu rearranged his schedule to meet late Tuesday afternoon with Clinton's November 5 election opponent, Republican nominee Bob Dole.

Dole, far behind Clinton in opinion polls and edged into the shadows by the eruption of this crisis, issued a statement on Monday saying, "Our friend Israel must not be asked to make concessions as a means of restoring order."

Democrat Clinton needed to walk a diplomatic and political tightrope in hosting this summit, balancing neutrality among the contending Middle East parties with sensitivity for the outlook of American Jews, a potent U.S. voting bloc.
White House spokesman Mike McCurry described Clinton as "determined." "It's not possible at this moment to be encouraged. But it is necessary to be determined," he said.

Clinton began his mediation effort with separate meetings -- set for 30 minutes, but involving a U.S. leader notorious for ignoring schedules -- Netanyahu and Arafat, followed by a group session including the King in the afternoon.

Arafat arrived in Washington about 5 a.m. EDT (0900 GMT) after stops in Egypt and Europe for talks with Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak -- who declined to attend the summit -- and European ministers.

Arafat met privately in Washington with Egyptian Foreign Minister Amr Moussa before the White House meetings. Moussa was representing Mubarak in Washington during the summit although he was not taking a direct part in the talks.

En route to Washington, Arafat told reporters he would attend the Washington summit with "no conditions or ultimatums." But there were unconfirmed reports in Israel that he had sent a letter to Clinton listing five demands.
Follow-on talks were to occur later on Tuesday and Wednesday at the White House and Blair House, a government guest house for distinguished foreign visitors just across Pennsylvania Avenue.

U.S. officials said all sides agreed to hold public statements to a minimum to try to encourage progress. "A very serious and a very delicate piece of business lies ahead in the next day and a half, and public pronouncements can tend to complicate the work that has to be done directly by the parties," McCurry said.

U.S. officials played down chances for a dramatic breakthrough in the talks, which followed the deaths of at least fifty-five Palestinians and 14 Israelis in five days of clashes after Israel opened a tunnel to archaeological sites near Jerusalem's Temple Mount, sacred in Judaism and Islam.

"It's clear to me that the Middle East peace process is in a state of crisis," said Secretary of State Warren Christopher, who has devoted much of his energies to trying to end the region's ancient strife.
Christopher said the goal of the summit was to convince the parties "to talk together again" and "find the basis for resuming negotiations" on stalled peace efforts.
Clinton's room for manoeuvre was limited by the pressures of the election campaign and Dole's staking out of a stance strongly sympathetic with Israel.
Dole campaign aides made it clear that they were ready to accuse Clinton of a major foreign policy fumble if the summit failed.

Ironically, the summit opened almost a year to the day after another Washington summit on the Middle East at which Rabin sealed a deal with Arafat that set out specific steps to implement the framework peace agreement signed in 1993.
One month later Rabin was assassinated.

McCurry all but ruled out the possibility that the summit would lead to marathon negotiations like the 1978 Camp David talks that produced as framework for peace between Israel and Egypt, saying "that's not a likely format for pursuing this."
